item.title: DRUA WOMEN’S AWARD I Drua Women hailed for inspiring a nation despite the loss
item.description: THE McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women may have fallen one step short of the Super Rugby Women’s title this season. Fijian Drua chief executive officer Jeff Miller believes the team’s greatest achievement extends far beyond the rugby field.
item.content:encoded:
THE McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women may have fallen one step short of the Super Rugby Women’s title this season.

Fijian Drua chief executive officer Jeff Miller believes the team’s greatest achievement extends far beyond the rugby field.

Speaking during the Drua Women’s Annual Presentation Night at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa in Nadi on Tuesday night, Miller praised the players for delivering a season that had inspired a nation and transformed lives.

He reminded the audience that the club’s vision was built on three pillars – winning Super Rugby titles, inspiring a nation and changing lives for the better.

While the elusive championship slipped away in the home grand final against the NSW Waratahs, Miller said the team had achieved the other two goals in remarkable fashion.

“What you’ve achieved this year is nothing short of extraordinary,” he said.

“You’ve won a Super Rugby minor premiership, you’ve inspired a nation and you’ve changed lives for the better.”

Miller highlighted the historic achievement of Fiji hosting its first-ever Super Rugby Women’s grand final, describing it as a milestone for women’s rugby in Fiji. More than 4,000 spectators packed the venue, setting a new attendance record for a standalone women’s rugby match in Fiji.

He said everyone associated with the club should be proud of the landmark occasion.

“It showed that the team has captured the hearts of our people,” Miller said.

He added that young girls across Fiji now had role models they could identify with players from villages just like theirs who had proven it was possible to compete on rugby’s biggest stage.

“That is changing lives for the better,” he said. Miller thanked head coach Mike Legge and the coaching and management staff for guiding the team through another memorable campaign before paying tribute to the players.

“You truly are a special group,” he said.

“You’ve represented your families, your villages, your supporters and most importantly your country with humility, courage and pride.”

He said their dedication, belief in one another and relentless work ethic had inspired thousands of young girls to dream bigger, adding that this could become the team’s greatest legacy.

item.title: DRUA WOMEN’S AWARD I Naihamu crowned with top Drua honour
item.description: FOR Josivini Naihamu, the McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women’s Awards was more than a celebration of an outstanding season. The 2026 awards night was the reward for years of sacrifice, faith and unwavering family support.
item.content:encoded:
FOR Josivini Naihamu, the McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women’s Awards was more than a celebration of an outstanding season.

The 2026 awards night was the reward for years of sacrifice, faith and unwavering family support.

The soft-spoken forward from Vagadra village in Nadroga, who also has maternal links to Nalele in Malomalo, walked away as the biggest winner of the night after claiming the prestigious McDonald’s Fiji Player of the Year award.

Her remarkable season was further recognised with the Encore Players’ Player of the Year award, voted by her teammates, and the Fiji Airways Try of the Year award for her spectacular finish, ahead of fellow nominees Aqela Raitubu and Kolora Lomani.

Despite her stellar campaign, Naihamu admitted the honours came as a complete surprise. “I am nervous and excited but thankful for this opportunity and the players and the staff for choosing me as a player,” she said moments after receiving the awards.

“I only know that I gave my all throughout the season, but I didn’t know that I would get the Player of the Year.”

Those words perfectly reflect the humility that has made Naihamu one of the Drua’s brightest young stars.

A former student of Swami Vivekananda College, Naihamu comes from a family where rugby is deeply rooted. With two brothers playing professional rugby overseas, the sport has always been part of her upbringing.

While the awards recognise what she has achieved in 2026, Naihamu believes her journey is only beginning.

She revealed that her biggest achievement this season has been opening doors to opportunities beyond Fiji.

“I played my heart out to get some of the opportunities from outside the world,” she said.

“I’m looking forward to some opportunities that are coming and I’m still praying for some other opportunities.”

Her rapid rise is also becoming a source of inspiration for young girls across the country, particularly those who dream of wearing the Drua jersey one day.

Naihamu encouraged aspiring female players to embrace rugby, saying the game can change lives in ways they may never imagine.

“To my younger sisters who are planning to play rugby, yes, it’s a good option. It can take you to places you never dreamed of, so you can choose rugby.”

Behind every success story, however, is a support system that keeps the dream alive.

For Naihamu, that unwavering support comes from home.

Whether watching her on television when the Drua play overseas or travelling to the grounds to cheer her on in Fiji, her family has been with her every step of the way.

Asked who she wanted to dedicate her awards to; there was no hesitation.

“Firstly, to my family back at home for the love, support and the prayers,” she said.

“When we go out to play in overseas, they watch me on the television and if we play here back at home they will come.

Still only at the beginning of what promises to be a bright career, Naihamu has already shown that talent, humility and faith can be a powerful combination.

Her unforgettable 2026 season has not only earned her the Drua’s highest individual honour but has also announced the arrival of another proud Nadroga rugby star chasing even greater dreams on the world stage.

McDonald’s Fiji managing director Marc McElrath, (left), presents the 2026 McDonald’s Fiji Player of the Year award to Josivini Naihamu during the McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women’s team awards night held at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa in Denarau Nadi on July 28, 2026.

Fiji Airways executive manager of Marketing and Brand Christina Templin (left) present the 2026 Fiji Airways Try of the Year award to Josivini Naihamu during the McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women’s team awards night held at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa in Denarau, Nadi on July 28, 2026.

item.title: DRUA WOMEN’S AWARD I An impactful season for the Drua women
item.description: THE McDonald’s Fiji Drua Women celebrated another chapter in the club’s history at their Annual Presentation Night at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa on Tuesday night. The glittering evening brought together players, staff members, partners and supporters to celebrate an unforgettable 2026 season where the Drua Women made 4th Grand Finals.
item.content:encoded:
THE McDonald’s Fiji Drua Women celebrated another chapter in the club’s history at their Annual Presentation Night at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa on Tuesday night.

The glittering evening brought together players, staff members, partners and supporters to celebrate an unforgettable 2026 season where the Drua Women made 4th Grand Finals.

This year saw the Drua Women finish the regular season as Minor Premiers for only the second time and created history in bringing home the Super Rugby Women grand final.

The evening culminated with six prestigious awards presented to those who made an outstanding impact throughout the season.

The awards include the Punjas Community Champion Award, 2026 Encore Players’ Player of the Year Award, 2026 Mogul Fan Player of the Year Award, the Rooster Chicken Rookie of the Year Award, Fiji Airways Try of the Year Award and the McDonald’s Player of the Year Award.

While the McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women fell short of lifting the Super Rugby Women’s title, team manager Eleina McDonald believes the squad’s greatest victory came long before the grand final whistle. Reflecting on the club’s 2026 campaign, McDonald said the players underwent an extraordinary transformation during a demanding 13-week season that not only shaped them into grand finalists but also stronger women on and off the field.

“The Super W season has only been 13 weeks, and we knew it was going to be a short but very impactful season,” McDonald said.

“Thirteen weeks can go by very quickly when you’re driven to get results, but it’s been absolutely rewarding and absolutely amazing.”

The campaign began immediately after many players helped Fiji win the Oceania Women’s Championship before transitioning into the professional environment of the Drua franchise.

McDonald said the adjustment from representing the national side to joining a professional club demanded more than simply improving rugby skills.

“This is a team that came straight out of the Oceania Women’s Championship and into the Drua Club. They were moving from one environment to another, but always with the intention of progressing to the next level.”

She believes the players embraced the challenge and developed rapidly throughout the season.

“I can honestly say they’ve grown. They’ve become more confident, they’ve learned more about each other, and it’s made them a stronger team.”

Although the Drua’s fairytale run ended with defeat in the grand final, McDonald said reaching the championship match and hosting the final on home soil highlighted just how much the squad had achieved.

“It wasn’t the performance we wanted in the final, and the girls know that, but in 13 weeks they’ve managed to connect as rugby sisters.”

Fijian Drua CEO Jeff Miller acknowledged the girls for their tremendous effort and dedication to the club throughout the season and how they have created history for Fiji’s women in rugby.

“For the first time ever in the history of women in rugby in Fiji, these Drua girls have achieved a significant milestone on bringing to Fiji the Super Rugby Women grand final and I applaud them for that,” Miller said.

Head coach Mike Legge commends the girls for their endless effort, commitment, dedication and their courage throughout the season.

“I am massively proud of the girls. It is a really moving faith for us, not just for the Drua but for Fiji as well,” Legge said.

Team manager Eleina McDonald also urged rugby supporters to continue backing women’s sport, saying encouragement from fans was more valuable than anything else.

“Twenty years ago, we were just fighting to tell people we were girls who wanted to play rugby.

“Now these girls are showing everyone what women can do. Love the sport, support the athletes and support women’s rugby. It’s not about the money; it’s about the support.”

In an emotional message to her players, McDonald reminded them that their journey was only beginning.

“They’ve become more empowered and they need to know we’ll always have their backs.

“As long as they stay united, stay disciplined and live the Drua values of Discipline, Resilience, United and Attitude, they’ll accomplish everything they set out to achieve.”

item.content:encoded:
A COLOUR story is the idea of repeating one colour in every room to create a subtle connection that brings your home together. You might have heard of the ‘red thread’ theory? Well, this is a similar concept, but a colour story goes much deeper.

Don’t worry, this doesn’t mean painting every room in the same colour – it’s about creating a sense of connection by introducing a colour (or finish) into every space, but in different ways.

Before we dive into tone, it might be handy to define what the word ‘tone’ really means. ‘Tone’ refers to when grey is added to create a variation of a colour. It can also be used to describe the lightness or darkness of a colour. While the ‘colour’ or ‘hue’ is blue, a blue tone could be a light blue, a mid-blue or a dark blue.

Repeat your colour in different places and proportions in every room, making your connection subtle. So let’s say your colour story is green. Your front door facing into the hallway is painted green; perhaps your downstairs loo is colour-drenched in green paint, and then you have a couple of green accents in the living room, such as a footstool, artwork or even a picture frame.

Your colour story can manifest in anything – rugs, cushions, curtains, tiles, paint, furniture – you name it, you can do it.

They might even manifest in undertones. You could have a different wall colour for every room, but they all share the same undertone. For example, a warm, yellow-based pink in the living room, a yellow-based white in the kitchen and a yellow-based green in the hallway will naturally harmonise.

Think of it like little connectors that run throughout your home to pull it all together, without having to use the same wall colour in each space or feel restricted to a single colour palette.

Transitional spaces, such as hallways, landings, and entryways, are also great places to reinforce your colour story without overwhelming the eye.

Flow isn’t just about colour. It’s about creating consistency through textures, materials, lighting, and decor. Your colour story might not even be a colour at all. It could be a type of wood or metal finish, or consistent flooring that guides you from room to room, creating a quiet sense of continuity.

item.title: LEADERSHIP FIJI I Inspiring others to succeed and give back
item.description: WHEN Dr Ricky Ram joined Leadership Fiji as part of the 2014 cohort, he simply saw it as an opportunity worth exploring. After being in the public service for many years, he had no idea how much taking up the program would shape the way he viewed leadership, service and his own purpose.
item.content:encoded:
WHEN Dr Ricky Ram joined Leadership Fiji as part of the 2014 cohort, he simply saw it as an opportunity worth exploring.

After being in the public service for many years, he had no idea how much taking up the program would shape the way he viewed leadership, service and his own purpose.

“For me, an opportunity to be part of Leadership Fiji came my way and I took it up,” he recalled.

What followed was an experience that challenged his thinking from the very first workshop.

“From the first few meetings, my eyes were opened and things I experienced were just amazing.”

That first impression marked the beginning of a journey that would bolster not only his leadership style but also the way he serves his community today.

For Dr Ram, Leadership Fiji has been more than just workshops and networking.

“It was about learning alongside people from different backgrounds and working together on a shared vision that addressed real community issues.”

His cohort focused on understanding the challenges faced by persons with disabilities in Fiji.

Visiting communities across the Northern Division opened his eyes to the barriers many people continue to face every day.

The experience stayed with him long after the program ended.

Today, through his dental clinic in the Hidden Paradise of Savusavu, Dr Ram has been able to provide some free dental treatment for patients with disabilities.

“It’s been a good way to give back to the community because at times we are just focused on the business and work aspect of things. ”

“Leadership Fiji reminded us that we also have to give something back to the community that we are part of and/or has made us successful.”

In the end, what began as a Leadership Fiji project has become a lasting commitment to serving some of the community’s most vulnerable members.

One of the biggest lessons Dr Ram took away from Leadership Fiji was the importance of working with others.

“For many years, I’d been working in isolation,” he said.

“Leadership Fiji taught me the value of collaboration and working together.”

Building strong networks, he explained, allowed leaders to achieve far more than they would on their own.

“It’s always good to have a good network. It really streamlines things and you’re able to achieve much more. In isolation, you wouldn’t really be able to achieve a lot.”

The program also strengthened his communication skills and taught him the importance of approaching challenges with the right mindset.

Just as importantly, it reminded him to slow down.

“Sometimes we just have to learn to be grateful for the things around us and give ourselves a break from all the work that we do so we can recharge ourselves before continuing.”

Leadership Fiji also helped Dr Ram better understand his own purpose as a leader.

“I think there’s been a boost in my confidence level,” he said.

“It has enabled me to see the purpose that I have and what I’m actually trying to achieve. That’s much more streamlined for me now.”

Rather than changing how he interacts with patients, colleagues and the wider community, he believes the program has strengthened the relationships he had already been building.

“It has not only really changed it, it has strengthened it too.”

The disability project remains one of the most meaningful parts of Dr Ram’s Leadership Fiji experience. Travelling through the Northern Division, the team witnessed firsthand how difficult everyday life can be for persons with disabilities.

“It was sad to see the level of community engagement,” he reflected.

item.title: PACIFIC FIBER CONFERENCE I AI threats
item.description: PACIFIC enterprises must shift from traditional cybersecurity to complete digital and cyber resilience to survive an era where artificial intelligence is weaponising cyber threats, a conference in Nadi was told. Speaking at the Pacific Fiber Conference 2026 at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Resort and Spa, Field CISCO and head of Cybersecurity Product at Philippines Telco Alexis Bernardino warned that leg
item.content:encoded:
PACIFIC enterprises must shift from traditional cybersecurity to complete digital and cyber resilience to survive an era where artificial intelligence is weaponising cyber threats, a conference in Nadi was told.

Speaking at the Pacific Fiber Conference 2026 at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Resort and Spa, Field CISCO and head of Cybersecurity Product at Philippines Telco Alexis Bernardino warned that legacy security practices are no longer enough to protect critical infrastructure.

“Now, resiliency is no longer a security KPI because right now, we are saying we need to be resilient, but no, it is now a business survival metric for all of us, for all of Fiji and the rest of the Pacific.”

Mr Bernadino highlighted significant advancements in frontier AI models released early this year that possess autonomous vulnerability discovery capabilities.

“During internal testing across major operating systems, thousands of zero day vulnerabilities surfaced, including flaws dating back three decades that had never been detected.

“Over 99 per cent of those discovered vulnerabilities were unpatched.”

Mr Bernardino said between February and April 2026, within a 60-day window, vulnerability exploit generation increased.

“In 2018, it took merely 2.3 years before a certain vulnerability could be exploited, but now in 2026, because of this development, it goes down to 16 hours.

“Meaning, before even the CVE is published for companies to patch it, it has been exploited already. Traditional patching is already obsolete.”

Mr Bernardino urged Pacific organisations and telecommunication operators to adopt active defence frameworks, build resilient multi-data centre architectures, and merge network and security operations into unified resilience operation centres.

He said these measures align with Fiji’s Cybercrime Act 2021 and the national cybersecurity strategy for digital acceleration, ensuring critical business and national infrastructure remain operational even while under attack.

item.title: PEOPLE CENTRED I Ocean of Peace – The Papua the world rarely sees

item.content:encoded:
BEFORE sunrise on an August morning, a schoolyard in Papua begins to stir. A teacher checks the line of students rehearsing for the flag ceremony. Nearby, young people fasten red-and-white decorations to bamboo poles. Mothers arrange food for a community gathering, while children practise games they have waited all year to play. Somewhere in the background, a church choir rehearses a hymn of thanksgiving.

By midday, the field will be filled with laughter, music and families. Traditional dress will appear alongside the national colours. Local languages will flow easily through the crowd. Elders will watch as children dance, race and sing. The scene will be unmistakably Papuan and unmistakably part of Indonesia’s Independence Day.

Yet this is rarely the Papua the world sees.

For many people outside the region, Papua is encountered mainly through reports of political dispute, armed violence, security operations and competing claims about its future. Those issues are real and should not be dismissed. But when they become the only lens through which Papua is viewed, millions of ordinary lives disappear behind the headline.

Every August, another picture comes into focus.

From Jayapura on the Pacific coast to Merauke in the far south, from Wamena in the highlands to Timika, Biak and Sorong, preparations for August 17 take shape in schools, churches, neighbourhoods and villages. Students rehearse ceremonies. Youth groups decorate streets. Congregations gather in prayer. Community organisations prepare cultural performances, local food and competitions that bring neighbours together.

These celebrations are not spectacles designed for foreign audiences. Most will never be filmed by an international broadcaster or quoted in a political statement. They continue because communities themselves organise them, year after year, as part of the rhythm of local life.

A child carrying a flag almost as tall as he is does not imagine that he is making a geopolitical argument. A mother straightening her daughter’s ceremonial uniform is not performing for a camera. A customary elder watching grandchildren dance is not reading from a government script. They are taking part in moments that are familiar, local and deeply human.

That matters because Papua is too often discussed as an abstraction. It becomes a territory on a map, a diplomatic issue or a contest between rival narratives. The people who live there are then reduced to symbols selected by one side or another.

But Papua is not an abstraction to the teacher preparing tomorrow’s lesson, the fisherman leaving before dawn, the farmer tending a garden, the trader opening a market stall, the pastor visiting a family or the parent hoping a child will have better opportunities. Their daily concerns are not so different from those of families elsewhere in the Pacific.

For Fiji, this is worth reflecting upon through the vision of the Pacific as an Ocean of Peace. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s idea asks the region to build peace through trust, dialogue and mutual respect. It also asks something more difficult: the willingness to see neighbouring societies in their full complexity, rather than through the most dramatic images available to us.

Peace begins with accuracy. It is difficult to understand a society fairly when conflict is treated as its permanent condition and ordinary life as an exception. In reality, it is ordinary life that carries a community from one day to the next.

Papua’s Independence Day celebrations do not erase indigenous identity. One only has to look at the celebrations themselves. Papuan languages are spoken. Traditional music is played. Indigenous dances take centre stage. Local food is shared. Customary leaders remain respected. The red-and-white flag does not require these communities to leave their culture at the gate. Their culture enters the celebration with them.

This coexistence may appear inconvenient to those who prefer simple political categories. Yet human identity is rarely simple. A person can be deeply rooted in a clan, a church, a language, a town and a nation at the same time. These loyalties do not always cancel one another.

An honest view of Papua must also acknowledge that the region contains different political opinions, experiences and grievances. No serious observer should pretend otherwise. Development gaps, inequality, violence and distrust deserve sober attention, and civilian safety must remain central to every discussion.

But honesty cannot stop there. Diversity of opinion also means that no single activist, political group, armed organisation or government official can speak for every Papuan. The most visible voice is not necessarily the most representative, and the loudest moment is not necessarily the most typical.

Fijians understand this instinctively. No one would claim to know Fiji by looking only at its political crises while ignoring daily life in Suva, Lautoka, Labasa, Levuka or the outer islands. Such a portrait might contain facts, but it would still be false in its incompleteness. It would miss the schools, markets, churches, villages, friendships and family obligations through which the country is actually lived.

This does not mean turning away from difficult questions. It means refusing to let difficult questions erase everything else. Journalism should report conflict, but audiences should remember that conflict is an event, not an entire people. Political debate may shape perceptions of Papua, but it does not wake children for school, put food on tables or sustain communities through grief and celebration.

On 17 August, many of those communities will gather again. Some will begin with prayer. Some will stand for a flag ceremony. Some will celebrate through football, sack races, music or traditional dance. Small businesses will sell food and handicrafts. Families will take photographs. Children will return home tired, carrying small prizes and stories they will repeat until next year’s celebration.

Long after the speeches have ended, the most enduring image may be the simplest: a child running across a field with a red-and-white flag in one hand, while a parent calls from the edge of the crowd and an elder smiles nearby.

There is nothing dramatic enough in that scene to become breaking news.

Papua is not only the place where political arguments occur. It is also a place where people teach, worship, trade, farm, fish, raise families, preserve their traditions and celebrate together. Its future will be shaped not only by those who issue statements or carry weapons, but by the millions who quietly build community every day.

Perhaps it is time the Pacific also saw the other.

This commentary draws on publicly available information from Indonesia’s Badan Pusat Statistik (BPS), UNESCO, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the World Bank, the Australian National University’s Department of Pacific Affairs, the International Crisis Group, the University of Papua (UNIPA), and Indonesia’s Ministry of Education, Culture, Research and Technology. These sources provide data and research on Papua’s demographic diversity, indigenous cultures, human development, education, governance and regional affairs, recognising both the region’s challenges and the everyday lives of its communities.

item.title: PERSPECTIVE I Crime, drugs and squatters
item.description: Several years ago, while living in Bayview Heights, one of my neighbours was burgled. Police arrived with a sniffer dog, which picked up the scent and tracked it down the road to a nearby squatter settlement. When officers entered the settlement and questioned residents, nobody was willing to identify the suspects. Whether it was fear, loyalty or simply a refusal to cooperate, the investigation re
item.content:encoded:
Several years ago, while living in Bayview Heights, one of my neighbours was burgled. Police arrived with a sniffer dog, which picked up the scent and tracked it down the road to a nearby squatter settlement. When officers entered the settlement and questioned residents, nobody was willing to identify the suspects. Whether it was fear, loyalty or simply a refusal to cooperate, the investigation reached a dead end. After speaking with police officers that day, and on subsequent occasions, I came to understand that this was not an isolated incident. It appeared to be a commonly occurring theme.

ACROSS the Suva-Nausori corridor, police are regularly called to investigate crimes that eventually lead them into squatter settlements. Law enforcement officers also conduct frequent drug operations in squatter settlements as Fiji grapples with an escalating drug crisis.

Now, I am in no way saying that every single person living in a squatter settlement is involved in drugs and crime.

But many squatter settlements have become environments where drugs and crime flourish, where criminals can hide more easily, and where police operations become more difficult.

Fiji’s squatter settlement problem has grown rapidly over the past two decades.

Government reports estimate that around one quarter of Fiji’s urban population now lives in more than 200 squatter settlements, most of them concentrated around the Suva-Nausori corridor and other urban centres.

We should be honest about what squatting is. It is, by definition, the unlawful occupation of land. Compassion for those facing hardship does not change that legal reality.

This crisis did not emerge overnight. It is, in large part, a legacy of the former FijiFirst Government, whose failure to confront the growth of illegal settlements allowed the problem to deepen.

Today, there are renewed calls to provide electricity, water and other services to settlements that remain unlawful. One has to ask: have political votes become more important than tackling the growing problems of drugs, crime and the increasing strain on Fiji’s infrastructure?

There is also an issue of fairness that is rarely discussed. Families who obey the law must pay rent or mortgages, rates, utilities and the many costs of living in Fiji’s urban centres. Those occupying land illegally avoid many of these costs, effectively allowing them to live beyond their means while enjoying the same access to jobs and services.

Worse still, this privilege is sometimes exploited. In 2019, a newspaper investigation revealed that some occupants of squatter settlements were renting out rooms, extending their homes to accommodate paying tenants and even selling structures built on land they did not legally own.

There is also the issue of urban capacity. Every new squatter settlement places additional pressure on roads, water supply, electricity networks, waste management, schools and healthcare services. Infrastructure designed for one population must suddenly serve many more people, often without the corresponding investment needed to support that growth. The result is declining service quality that affects everyone.

Crime is another consequence that cannot be ignored. Fiji Police statistics show theft, burglary and drug offences have all increased in recent years, while national drug cases have risen sharply, driven particularly by methamphetamine and marijuana.

Squatter settlements have become a convenient cover for criminal activity, allowing offenders to hide among densely populated communities and making police investigations more difficult. Academic research in Fiji has also identified some settlements as developing reputations as crime “hotspots.”

Perhaps the greatest cost is to the rule of law itself. When governments tolerate the illegal occupation of land for years on end, they send the message that some laws can simply be ignored if enough time passes or enough political pressure is applied.

Brazil’s favelas provide one example that should have Fijians very worried.

Many began as small squatter communities built by people with nowhere else to live.

Over time, they evolved into densely populated neighbourhoods where organised crime and drug trafficking gained influence, making effective policing increasingly difficult.

Fiji is heading down this road. While we are not yet facing the scale of Brazil’s favelas, the warning signs are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. If the growth of illegal settlements continues unchecked, accompanied by rising drug activity, crime and mounting pressure on public infrastructure, the challenge will only become more difficult and more expensive to solve.

Ignoring illegal settlements will not make them disappear. Romanticising them will not solve the problems they create.

This is a real and growing problem that Fiji can no longer afford to ignore.

We need leaders with the courage to make difficult decisions in the national interest, not politicians willing to sacrifice the country’s future for a few thousand votes. If we fail to act now, the price paid by future generations will be far greater than the political cost of acting today.
